provenance.method: Raw UMI counts (layers/UMIs) summed per donor per cell type, divided by that donor's total UMIs in the same cell type, times one million. Cell-type share: a neuronal type (Sst, L2/3 IT, L5 IT) as a percentage of that donor's neuronal nuclei, a non-neuronal type (microglia-PVM, oligodendrocyte, astrocyte) as a percentage of that donor's non-neuronal nuclei, split by SEA-AD's own Class label. provenance.nucleiNote: Every nucleus in the 84 donors' final-nuclei objects is counted: all of them feed the neuron and non-neuronal denominators.

poll.framing: Six statements. Go with your gut.

items.statement: Dementia is a disease of the brain
items.why: Dementia is caused by diseases that damage brain cells.
It comes from physical damage to the brain, not from a mental health condition.

items.statement: Dementia is a normal process of ageing
items.why: Most older people never get it. Age raises the risk but does not cause it.

items.statement: Dementia is another term for Alzheimer’s Disease
items.why: Dementia is the set of symptoms. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause.

items.statement: There are many different kinds of dementia
items.why: Alzheimer’s is one. Vascular, Lewy body and frontotemporal dementia are others.

items.statement: People who eat healthily and exercise are less likely to get dementia
items.why: A healthy lifestyle lowers the risk. It does not remove it.

caseStudies.title: Sst inhibitory interneurons
caseStudies.pickerLine: Do these neurons become rarer as Alzheimer’s pathology builds up?
caseStudies.measurePhrase: the share of neurons that are Sst neurons

intro.background: Neurons do not only switch each other on. Some switch others off, which keeps brain activity balanced. One family of these inhibitory neurons is called Sst neurons.
intro.known: In Alzheimer’s disease, some brain networks become overactive. Researchers suspect that losing inhibitory neurons could be part of the reason.
intro.gap: If that is right, Sst neurons should be rarer in brains with more Alzheimer’s pathology. Is that what the data shows?

aims.aim: To find out whether Sst neurons make up a smaller share of neurons in donors with more Alzheimer’s pathology.
aims.h0: The share of neurons that are Sst neurons is the same in {{firstGroup}} donors and {{lastGroup}} donors.
aims.question: What do you predict for {{lastGroup}} donors compared with {{firstGroup}} donors?

h1.up: Sst neurons are a higher share of neurons in {{lastGroup}} donors.
h1.same: Sst neurons are the same share of neurons in both groups.
h1.down: Sst neurons are a lower share of neurons in {{lastGroup}} donors.

methods.participants: {{donorTotal}} people donated their brains to research after they died. Pathologists scored each brain for amyloid plaques and tau tangles and placed it in one of four levels, from Not AD to High.
methods.tissue: Scientists took a small piece from the middle temporal gyrus, a region of the cortex on the side of the brain.
methods.measure: For each donor, we count the Sst neurons and divide by all of that donor’s neurons. The result is a percentage: the Sst share.
methods.analysis: Each donor gives one value. We compare the middle value (the median) in {{firstGroup}} donors with the median in {{lastGroup}} donors, using a Mann-Whitney U test, which compares two groups by rank. We call a difference significant if p is below 0.05.

check.wrong: Not here. Cells from the same person are alike, so each donor is counted once.

caseStudies.title: Microglia and immune genes
caseStudies.pickerLine: Do immune cells turn up a risk gene when pathology builds up?

intro.background: Microglia are the brain’s immune cells. They patrol the tissue, clear away debris and gather around amyloid plaques.
intro.known: Two genes that microglia use, TREM2 and APOE, are linked to a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s disease. Certain versions of each gene raise that risk.
intro.gap: A gene that affects risk might also be more active where there is more pathology. Is TREM2 more active in the microglia of donors with high pathology?

aims.aim: To find out whether TREM2 is more active in microglia from donors with more Alzheimer’s pathology.
aims.h0: TREM2 activity in microglia is the same in {{firstGroup}} donors and {{lastGroup}} donors.
aims.question: What do you predict for {{lastGroup}} donors compared with {{firstGroup}} donors?

h1.up: TREM2 activity in microglia is higher in {{lastGroup}} donors.
h1.same: TREM2 activity in microglia is the same in both groups.
h1.down: TREM2 activity in microglia is lower in {{lastGroup}} donors.

methods.tissue: Scientists took a small piece from the middle temporal gyrus, a region of the cortex on the side of the brain.
methods.measure: A gene is active when a cell copies it into mRNA messages. For each donor, we count the TREM2 messages in their microglia, out of every million messages counted in those cells. The unit is counts per million.
methods.analysis: Each donor gives one value. We compare the middle value (the median) in {{firstGroup}} donors with the median in {{lastGroup}} donors, using a Mann-Whitney U test, which compares two groups by rank. We call a difference significant if p is below 0.05.

ucas.heading: UCAS and careers
ucas.intro: Nobody is born knowing how university applications work. Here is what people rarely say out loud.
ucas.statementIntro: Admissions tutors want to know what you did and what you learned. “I found it interesting” does not tell them.
ucas.weak: I did an online project about Alzheimer’s and found it interesting.
ucas.strong: Investigating single-nucleus transcriptomic data from the SEA-AD atlas, I analysed the selective vulnerability of SST inhibitory interneurons across Braak stages, developing skills in evaluating donor spread and confounding variables.
statementWhy: It names the data and the method.
It says exactly what was analysed.
It ends on a skill, not a feeling.
ucas.statementWarning: Do not copy this sentence. UCAS checks every application for matching text. Write about what you actually did, in your own words.
ucas.compHeading: Beyond medicine: what is computational biology?
comp: Biomedical research is not only lab coats and pipettes. A lot of it happens on a computer.
Computational biologists write code to find patterns in huge biological datasets, like the one on this site. The same skills power bioinformatics, health data science and AI in healthcare.
You can get there from biology, biochemistry, biomedical science, maths, computer science or physics. Entry requirements differ, so check each course on UCAS.

insights.myth: "Dementia and Alzheimer’s are the same thing."
insights.headline: Dementia is not one disease.
insights.body: [[Dementia]] is the name for a set of **symptoms**: memory loss, confusion and trouble with everyday tasks, getting worse over time. It is not a disease in itself. ==Several different brain diseases cause dementia.== **Alzheimer’s disease** is the most common of them.

discs.name: Alzheimer’s disease
discs.line: The most common cause. The one this site looks at.

discs.name: Vascular dementia
discs.line: Caused by reduced blood flow to the brain.

discs.name: Lewy body dementia
discs.line: Linked to protein deposits called Lewy bodies inside neurons.

discs.name: Frontotemporal dementia
discs.line: Damage starts in the front and side regions of the brain.

insights.alt: A ring labelled dementia, holding four labelled discs: Alzheimer’s disease, the largest, with vascular, Lewy body and frontotemporal dementia.

insights.myth: "Dementia is just part of getting old."
insights.headline: Alzheimer’s is a physical disease of brain cells.
insights.body: Your brain works because billions of [[neurons]] pass signals to each other. In Alzheimer’s disease, neurons slowly **stop working, lose their connections and die**. The damage begins long before any symptoms show. ==Pathologists can see this damage under a microscope and grade it==, from **Not AD** to **High**. That grade is called the [[pathology level]].

knot.label: Unravel this
knot.title: What do pathologists actually see?
knot.body: Clumps of two proteins that should not be there, called amyloid and tau. The more clumps, and the further they have spread, the higher the pathology level. Every chart in the lab sorts donors by this grade.

steps.caption: Amyloid builds up in the gaps between neurons.

insights.alt: A network of neurons. As the pathology level rises, links fade, neurons dim and immune cells gather.

insights.myth: "The brain is made of one kind of cell."
insights.headline: The brain is not one kind of cell.
insights.body: Neurons get the attention, but they are only part of the picture, and they are not all alike. {cell:l2-3-it|Excitatory neurons} **pass signals on**. {cell:sst|Inhibitory neurons} **calm signals down**. {cell:microglia-pvm|Microglia} are the brain’s **immune cells** and clear up damage. Support cells feed neurons and insulate their wiring. ==A disease can hit one type hard and leave its neighbour untouched.==

groups.job: Pass signals on, and link brain areas together.
Switch other neurons off, keeping activity balanced.
Patrol the brain and clear up debris.
Feed neurons and insulate their wiring.

knot.label: Unravel this
knot.title: Why does this matter?
knot.body: If you only measure the brain as a whole, a big loss in one small group of cells can vanish into the average. You will meet three of these cell types again in the lab.

insights.alt: Four labelled groups of cells: excitatory neurons with long links, inhibitory neurons with short blunt links, branching immune cells, and wrapping support cells.

insights.myth: "Scientists already know exactly how Alzheimer’s damages the brain."
insights.headline: Nobody knows yet which cells go first.
insights.body: Which cells are damaged **first**? Do immune cells **protect** the brain or make things worse? These are open questions that researchers are working on now. To answer them, they had to stop grinding tissue into one average. ==They started reading cells one at a time.== This is called [[single-cell sequencing]].

labels: One cell at a time: each type visible

insights.alt: The same cells shown twice: blurred into one grey average, and separated into their four coloured types.

contact.heading: The student behind Unravel
contact.intro: Unravel was built and is based off an Imperial College London student.
contact.name: Giulio Taggart
contact.role: Fourth and Final-year Biological Sciences BSc student at Imperial College London.
bio: I built Unravel because of two main things that I was not prepared for at university. One, learning how to write scientific reports. Two, understanding that a degree in Biology does not mean a career in the lab.
I want to help equip students for the transition into scientific writing and show them the power of computational Biology.
